widgets_values:
Invent an original, funny, engaging twelve-page picture book for ages 4-6 about a small woodland-garden mystery. Give Mia a concrete goal, meaningful choices, two purposeful funny failed ideas and a surprising earned resolution using a clue introduced early. The friends should have different personalities and useful contributions. Use lively read-aloud dialogue, sensory detail, varied sentence rhythms and a changing comic refrain. End with a specific warm or funny payoff, not a moral. No unexplained magic or additional named actors.
Exactly these three friends: Mia, a human child with short brown bobbed hair, a red hooded raincoat, blue denim dungarees, a pink undershirt and yellow wellington boots (110cm tall); Pip, an anthropomorphic cream rabbit with upright long ears, pink inner ears and nose, pale pink bare paws and feet, a short cream tail and blue buttoned waistcoat (50cm tall); Barnaby, an anthropomorphic grey fox with pointed muzzle, black nose, triangular ears with reddish-orange interiors, a white-tipped bushy tail, reddish-orange bare paws and feet and a yellow neckerchief (55cm tall). They walk on two legs. These are fictional physical proportions; keep their permanent designs and clothes throughout. Do not write design descriptions or measurements in the read-aloud prose.
Plan varied picture-book shots with AT MOST TWO visible characters in EVERY page illustration. The book still has all three friends: each supporting friend must appear in at least four illustrations, and include a scene of the two supporting friends together. The cover should show Mia alone with an intriguing setting or simple story clue. Set charactersPresent to exactly the figures visible in each image. A friend can be mentioned in the prose but outside the chosen shot. Every illustrated character must have a recognisable visible face.
Choose one clear, naturally drawable moment from each page's actual prose. Prefer a single primary visible action while the other character reacts naturally. Use common body movements and simple single-object interactions. Avoid intertwined bodies, one character carrying another, multiple characters manipulating the same object, ropes attached to moving loads, intricate fingertip contact or tails operating tools. These constraints apply while inventing the story; do not replace an already-written essential action with a different one. Keep the events playful and emotionally engaging, not a sequence of static poses.
Use at most one visually distinctive recurring manufactured object. When it recurs, repeat a short exact description of its shape, colour and material in every relevant image prompt, and keep its scale plausible and stable. All props are ordinary objects without faces. Do not require written words, labels or musical notation within the illustrations. Keep each page's visual action, emotional state, location, prop state and costume consistent with the words the child will hear.
Warm, hand-painted children's picture-book illustration, soft gouache and coloured-pencil texture, clear shapes, gentle lighting, a cohesive warm pastel palette.
